creedLine: I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.

cards.title: 1968 and 1989
cards.idea: After 1989 Christianity must find its voice: a privatized God “with nothing to do” leaves the world defenseless before technology and the loss of moral ground.
cards.before: Marxism collapsed in 1989 — why did the Christian message fail to step forward as the epoch-making alternative, and what does that failure reveal about how Christians had been living?
cards.after: Because believers had quietly lived etsi Deus non daretur, leaving God in the private realm with nothing to do. Only a faith that brings God into the public arena as judge, limit, and goal can speak to the new millennium.
cards.why: Ratzinger indicts not secularism but Christians: liberation theology’s God with nothing to do merely dramatized ordinary believers’ practical atheism. Yet the post-1989 hunger for religion shows the question of God cannot be suppressed.

cloze.pre: But the faith would really have come out of the ghetto only if it had brought its most distinctive feature with it into the public arena:
cloze.blank: the God who judges and suffers
cloze.post: , the God who sets limits and standards for us; the God from whom we come and to whom we are going.

cloze.pre: Yet God is
cloze.blank: “practical”
cloze.post: and not just some theoretical conclusion of a consoling world view that one may adhere to or simply disregard.

cloze.pre: But we ought to wonder whether God might not in fact be the genuine reality,
cloze.blank: the basic prerequisite for any “realism”
cloze.post: , so that, without him, nothing is safe.

cards.recall: Why does Ratzinger think the post-1989 rediscovery of religion still distorts Christianity, and what would a faith that has really “come out of the ghetto” look like in public life?

cards.title: Doubt and belief — man’s situation before the question of God
cards.idea: Believer and unbeliever both live in doubt: faith is never secure, unbelief never closes the question — “perhaps it is true” haunts both alike.
cards.before: When you picture someone who has lost faith, do you imagine a person at peace with a settled conclusion — or one who still hears the Rabbi’s “perhaps it is true”?
cards.after: Both are threatened: the believer by the plunge into unbelief, the unbeliever by the doubt that belief may after all be true. Doubt is the one avenue of communication between them.
cards.why: Ratzinger rejects the cozy clown-and-burning-village analogy: the problem is not outdated language but a shared abyss. It is only when belief is rejected that its “unrejectability” becomes evident.
cards.quote: It is not until belief is rejected that its unrejectability becomes evident.

cloze.pre: Fastened to the cross—with the cross
cloze.blank: fastened to nothing
cloze.post: , drifting over the abyss.

cloze.pre: Anyone who makes up his mind to evade the uncertainty of belief will have to experience
cloze.blank: the uncertainty of unbelief
cloze.post: , which can never finally eliminate for certain the possibility that belief may after all be the truth.

cloze.pre: Just as the believer knows himself to be constantly threatened by unbelief, which he must experience as a continual temptation, so for the unbeliever faith remains
cloze.blank: a temptation and a threat
cloze.post: to his apparently permanently closed world.

cards.recall: Explain in your own words why Ratzinger says that believer and unbeliever “share, each in his own way, doubt and belief”.

cards.title: The origin of belief — an attempt at a definition of belief
cards.idea: Belief is not inference but conversion: a second access to reality that trusts the unseen as the truly real — a leap, never demonstrable, renewed daily.
cards.before: Is believing mainly a matter of weighing evidence, or of the whole person turning around? What changes if “credo” names a basic behavior toward reality rather than an opinion?
cards.after: Credo is a fundamental option: the decision that the unseen is the truly real that supports all the rest of reality. Faith is conversion, an about-turn only he who turns about can receive.
cards.why: It is not self-evident that Christianity’s core word is credo: the Old Testament called itself “law”, Roman religion meant “rites”. Christianity stakes everything on belief — and belief is essentially an adventurous leap.
cards.quote: Belief has always had something of an adventurous break or leap about it

cloze.pre: But in this area of things that can be seen and grasped, the area that determines the living space of man, God
cloze.blank: does not occur and will never occur
cloze.post: , however much the area may be extended.

cloze.pre: It signifies the deliberate view that what cannot be seen, what can in no wise move into the field of vision, is not unreal; that, on the contrary, what cannot be seen in fact represents
cloze.blank: true reality
cloze.post: , the element that supports and makes possible all the rest of reality.

cloze.pre: Man’s natural inclination draws him to
cloze.blank: the visible
cloze.post: , to what he can take in his hand and hold as his own.

cards.recall: Why can faith never be “demonstrated”, and why does that not make it irrational or merely private?

cards.title: The dilemma of belief in the world of today
cards.idea: Modern unbelief hides the real scandal: faith seems to bind us to the past, yet beneath it lies Christianity’s positivism — God committed to one man, one moment.
cards.before: If the Gospel were safely timeless — a general wisdom about the Eternal — would believing be easier? What is actually lost when the “then” is dissolved into the “now”?
cards.after: The deepest offense is not antiquity but God’s self-commitment to history: the eternal entered one figure, one hour, so near that we can kill him. Interpretations that remove this offense are dishonest.
cards.why: Ratzinger calls this Christianity’s “ineradicable positivity”: revelation makes God touchable — and therefore killable. Modernizing revisions that avoid scandal trade the truth for a “viable proposition”.
cards.quote: God has come so near to us that we can kill him

cloze.pre: Belief appears no longer as the bold but challenging leap out of the apparent all of our visible world and into the apparent void of the invisible and intangible; it looks much more like
cloze.blank: a demand to bind oneself to yesterday
cloze.post: and to affirm it as eternally valid.

cloze.pre: The very thing that at first seems to bring God quite close to us, so that we can touch him as a fellow man, follow his footsteps and measure them precisely, also becomes in a very profound sense
cloze.blank: the precondition for the “death of God”
cloze.post: , which henceforth puts an ineradicable stamp on the course of history and the human relationship with God.

cloze.pre: An “interpreted” Christianity of this kind that has lost all contact with reality implies
cloze.blank: a lack of sincerity
cloze.post: in dealing with the questions of the non-Christian, whose “perhaps not” should worry us as seriously as we want the Christian “perhaps” to worry him.

cards.recall: What does Ratzinger mean by the “positivism” of Christianity, and why is a timeless or inoffensive version of the Gospel a kind of dishonesty?

cards.title: The boundary of the modern understanding of reality
cards.idea: Modern reason trusts only the made and the makable: Vico’s verum quia factum, then Marx’s faciendum. Belief stands on neither plane — truth is received, not manufactured.
cards.before: What counts as “real” for modern man: what can be measured and repeated, or what can be made to work? Where would belief fit into either scheme?
cards.after: Ratzinger traces two stages: truth reduced to what we have made (history), then to what we can make (technique). Belonging neither to know nor to make, belief lives in the relation stand–understand.
cards.why: Theology’s two rescue attempts — faith as history, then political theology as praxis — each smuggled faith onto the modern plane. Belief instead concerns basic decisions that no man can avoid making.
cards.quote: all that we can truly know is what we have made ourselves

cloze.pre: For the ancient world and the Middle Ages, being itself is true, in other words,
cloze.blank: apprehensible
cloze.post: , because God, pure intellect, made it, and he made it by thinking it.

cloze.pre: It comes to
cloze.blank: the primacy of the “makable” over the “made”
cloze.post: , for in fact what can man do with what has merely existed in the past?

cloze.pre: For when he says this, he is not primarily enunciating
cloze.blank: a program for changing the world
cloze.post: or simply attaching himself to a chain of historical events.

cards.recall: Summarize the two stages of the modern revolution in truth (factum, faciendum) and explain why belief cannot be placed on either plane.

cards.title: Faith as standing firm and understanding
cards.idea: Faith is standing firm on received ground: entrusting oneself to meaning one cannot make. Believing is literally taking a stand — and understanding grows only out of it.
cards.before: When you “believe” someone, are you less rational than when you verify a fact — or are you exercising a different, irreducible kind of reason?
cards.after: Belief is not incomplete knowledge but entrusting oneself to what was not made by us and yet upholds all our making. Meaning cannot be manufactured; it can only be received.
cards.why: From Isaiah 7:9 — “If you do not believe, then you do not abide” — Ratzinger draws the ‘mn (amen) root: truth, firm ground, trust. Believing is standing; only on that stand can understanding follow.
cards.quote: Meaning that is self-made is in the last analysis no meaning.

cloze.pre: Faith is thereby defined as
cloze.blank: taking up a position
cloze.post: , as taking a stand trustfully on the ground of the word of God.

cloze.pre: Essentially, it is
cloze.blank: entrusting oneself
cloze.post: to that which has not been made by oneself and never could be made and which precisely in this way supports and makes possible all our making.

cloze.pre: To try to manufacture it in this way, that is, out of the provable knowledge of what can be made, would resemble
cloze.blank: Baron Munchhausen’s absurd attempt
cloze.post: to pull himself up out of the bog by his own hair.

cards.recall: Explain the play on words Ratzinger finds in Isaiah 7:9 and the “amen” root, and why believing is a kind of standing rather than a kind of knowing.

cards.title: The rationality of faith
cards.idea: Faith’s “Amen” is no blind surrender: it entrusts itself to truth itself — the only ground man can stand on; understanding grows only out of belief.
cards.before: Is “Amen” a rational act or a leap in the dark? What does calculating knowledge give up in order to succeed — and what does faith refuse to give up?
cards.after: Amen means trusting a ground one did not make — a movement toward logos, meaning, truth. Calculating knowledge renounces the quest for truth itself; faith alone keeps meaning, ground, and truth indivisible.
cards.why: Ratzinger reverses the cliché: it is practical knowledge that is positivist and truth-renouncing, while faith is the quest for truth itself. Mystery is not an excuse for failed reason but the ground that comprehends us.
cards.quote: Truth is the only ground suitable for man to stand upon.

cloze.pre: Thus “Amen” simply says once again in its own way what belief means: the trustful placing of myself on
cloze.blank: a ground that upholds me
cloze.post: , not because I have made it and checked it by my own calculations but, rather, precisely because I have not made it and cannot check it.

cloze.pre: On the contrary, it is
cloze.blank: a movement toward the logos, the ratio
cloze.post: , toward meaning and so toward truth itself, for in the final analysis the ground on which man takes his stand cannot possibly be anything else but the truth revealing itself.

cloze.pre: It achieves its successes precisely by
cloze.blank: renouncing the quest for truth itself
cloze.post: and by directing its attention to the “rightness”, the “soundness” of the system whose hypothetical design must prove itself in the functioning of the experiment.

cards.recall: Why does Ratzinger say the “Amen” of faith is rational rather than blind, and what does calculating knowledge sacrifice that faith will not?

cards.title: “I believe in you”
cards.idea: Christian faith’s center is not “something” but “you”: in Jesus the meaning of the world is a person who knows and loves me — believing, trusting, loving are one.
cards.before: Could faith in “something” — a spiritual ground of the world — ever be enough? What changes when its object is not an idea but a person who addresses you?
cards.after: In Jesus faith finds a “you” that upholds me: objective meaning that knows me and loves me. All the theses of the Creed are expressions of this one about-turn.
cards.why: Even this personal faith keeps the question “Are you really he?” — asked even by John the Baptist. Love itself demands reflection; the whole book revolves around this question.
cards.quote: its central formula is not “I believe in something”, but “I believe in you.”

cloze.pre: It is
cloze.blank: the encounter with the man Jesus
cloze.post: , and in this encounter it experiences the meaning of the world as a person.

cloze.pre: Thus faith is the finding of a “you” that upholds me and amid all the unfulfilled—and in the last resort unfulfillable—hope of human encounters gives me
cloze.blank: the promise of an indestructible love
cloze.post: that not only longs for eternity but also guarantees it.

cloze.pre: Thus in the last analysis believing, trusting, and loving are one, and all the theses around which belief revolves are only
cloze.blank: concrete expressions of the all-embracing about-turn
cloze.post: , of the assertion “I believe in you”—of the discovery of God in the countenance of the man Jesus of Nazareth.

cards.recall: Why must faith’s object be a “you” rather than “something”, and why does love require the ever-repeated question “Are you really he?”

cards.title: History and structure of the Apostles’ Creed
cards.idea: The Creed began as a three-question baptismal dialogue in Rome, shaped by history: Western and Eastern creeds differ — salvation-history versus cosmic-metaphysical emphasis.
cards.before: Did the twelve apostles really each contribute an article to the Creed? What does its actual origin — the baptismal dialogue of Rome — tell us about what a creed is for?
cards.after: The Creed grew from the triple baptismal question and answer, refined over centuries; the apostolic-authorship story is a later legend. The Roman form stresses salvation-history, the East’s the cosmos and creation.
cards.why: Ratzinger hides none of the text’s messy history — imperial politics, East–West tension — yet insists it faithfully echoes the ancient Church’s faith, which in its kernel echoes the New Testament.
cards.quote: the oldest form of the confession of faith takes the shape of a tripartite dialogue

cloze.pre: In the East this Roman symbol or creed remained unknown; it came as no small surprise to the Roman representatives at
cloze.blank: the ecumenical Council of Florence
cloze.post: in the fifteenth century when they learned from the Greeks that the symbolum presumed to stem from the apostles was not employed by them.

cloze.pre: Very soon (probably still in the fifth century) this legend crystallized into the assumption that
cloze.blank: each of the twelve articles
cloze.post: into which the whole was now divided had been contributed by one of the twelve apostles.

cloze.pre: The East, on the other hand, has always sought to see the Christian faith in a cosmic and metaphysical perspective, which is mirrored in professions of faith above all by the fact that
cloze.blank: Christology and belief in creation are related to each other
cloze.post: , and thus the uniqueness of the Christian story and the everlasting, all-embracing nature of the creation come into close association.

cards.recall: How did the Apostles’ Creed actually take shape, and what do the differences between the Roman and Eastern creeds reveal about the faith they confess?

cards.title: Limits and meaning of the text
cards.idea: The Creed’s checkered history — unity, East–West split, imperial politics — is itself part of believing: faith happens on the petty human scale and so must include forgiveness.
cards.before: If the Creed was tangled up with imperial politics and regional power games, can it still carry the Gospel — or is that tangle part of what faith honestly is?
cards.after: The text’s history shows belief entering the world mingled with every human circumstance — the leap happens on the petty scale of everything human. So faith must have to do with forgiving.
cards.why: Instead of excusing the muddles, Ratzinger reads them as instruction: man is “a divided being pitiful in his greatness” and needs forgiveness even in his best and purest moments.
cards.quote: faith has to do, and must have to do, with forgiving

cloze.pre: First, the Creed
cloze.blank: cuts right across all cleavages and tensions
cloze.post: and expresses the common ground of belief in the triune God.

cloze.pre: Thus the fate of this text demonstrates how the answer to the call from Galilee mingles, at the moment of its entry into history, with
cloze.blank: all the human circumstances of man
cloze.post: : with the special interests of one region, with the estrangement of those called to unity among themselves, with the tricks of the powers of this world.

cloze.pre: Something absolutely central becomes visible here, namely, that faith has to do, and must have to do, with forgiving; that it aims at leading man to recognize that he is a being that can only find himself in
cloze.blank: the reception and transmission of forgiveness
cloze.post: , a being that needs forgiveness even in his best and purest moments.

cards.recall: Why does Ratzinger think the Creed’s entanglement with politics and division is not just a scandal to be explained away?

cards.title: Creed and dogma
cards.idea: Faith is not doctrine recited but conversion: the baptismal dialogue of renunciation and assent turns the whole person from the visible to the invisible — dogma serves this about-turn.
cards.before: Is “dogma” a list of propositions to be recited, or something that happens to a person? What were the first Christians actually doing when they said “Credo”?
cards.after: In baptism “I believe” answers “Do you believe?” after a triple renunciation: faith is a shift of the whole being, an about-turn one can render as “I hand myself over to”.
cards.why: Ratzinger prefers the original dialogue form even to the later “I” and “We” creeds: dogma grew from councils seeking right doctrine, but its birthplace is the conversion enacted in baptism.
cards.quote: The phrase “I believe” could here be literally translated by “I hand myself over to”, “I assent to”.

cloze.pre: This means that faith is located in
cloze.blank: the act of conversion
cloze.post: , in the turn of one’s being from worship of the visible and practicable to trust in the invisible.

cloze.pre: In the procedure of the threefold renunciation and the threefold assent, linked as it is with
cloze.blank: the thrice-repeated death symbol of drowning
cloze.post: and the thrice-repeated symbolization of resurrection to new life, the true nature of faith or belief is clearly illustrated: it is a conversion, an about-turn, a shift of being.

cloze.pre: This original form of the symbol, which consisted at first only of
cloze.blank: the two-in-oneness of question and answer
cloze.post: , seems to me to be a very much more accurate expression of the structure of faith than the later simplified, collective “I”-form.

cards.recall: Why does Ratzinger think the baptismal question-and-answer form expresses the nature of faith better than a list of doctrines — and what is dogma really for?

cards.title: The Creed as expression of the structure of faith
cards.idea: Faith comes from hearing, lives in the “We”, and is a symbolum — a broken half completed only with others: Church and word belong to the thing itself.
cards.before: Could you have faith as a solitary individual, privately searching for the truth? What changes when you learn that “symbol” literally means a broken piece of a ring?
cards.after: Faith comes from hearing, not private reflection; its word precedes thought and binds a community. As symbolon each believer holds only half — Church and confession belong to faith, not to it as add-ons.
cards.why: Ratzinger follows Marius Victorinus: Christianity is not Platonism, an idea for solitary minds, but a way. The believers’ “We” is not for small minds; it is in a certain sense the matter itself.
cards.quote: Christian belief is not an idea but life

cloze.pre: On the contrary, it is characteristic of faith that it comes from hearing, that it is
cloze.blank: the reception of something that I have not thought out
cloze.post: , so that in the last analysis thinking in the context of faith is always a thinking over of something previously heard and received.

cloze.pre: A symbolum is something that points to
cloze.blank: its complementary other half
cloze.post: and thus creates mutual recognition and unity.

cloze.pre: It also means that every man holds the faith only as a symbolon,
cloze.blank: a broken, incomplete piece
cloze.post: that can only attain unity and completeness when it is laid together with the others.

cards.recall: Explain the etymology of “symbolum” and why Ratzinger concludes that the Church and common confession belong to the nature of faith rather than being added to it.
